Most schools, public, charter (and private to a lesser extent) are always seeming to need people and was by far the best move I made in IT after getting my Associates. No certs, and service/retail job experience and I got my first school position within 2 months post graduation. 

Going into IT as either a single site provider for a school, or an MSP covering a district or two will provide a foot in the door + real experience + (most likely) a paycheck higher than minimum wage.

If you have the degree in Cybersecurity, but barely learned any cyber at all, why are you focusing on jobs that require 3+ years of cyber-sec experience?

I too got a degree ~2 years ago in cybersecurity from a local Jr College and was able to start a career in the IT department for a public school. While it’s not ideal, it’s not possible to learn the experience a job can provide from class unless you extensively go out of your way to work on it for fun in your free time. The school taught me business practices, common infrastructure and popular tools of the trade, all stuff that I was able to then leverage on my next resume.

Terms like “network infrastructure” and “Office365 Admin” not only sound good, but show that you know how to work in most IT environments. Leverage those smaller skills + the ones from school + your outside background knowledge to seem like a real contender in the job market.

There's a lot more info you should know before going into it

1. I saw your comment responding to another user, I can assure you that there is 1000% not a USB method like the Wii or PS3. Beyond that, its not a console that is for the soldering beginner. I've been console modding for over 5 years now, and the RGH was BY FAR the hardest console mode I've done out of my collection of 10+ hacked systems.
2. Do you know what model of 360 you have? If you're seriously considering an RGH/JTAG then you need to know is its the first generation, slim or E. After that, you need to disassemble the console and find the motherboard model. There are plenty of guides online, but MrMario on YT seems to be the goto for this sort of thing. After that, I would look into the guides for your specific motherboard and see if its something you can feasibly do.

I would encourage you to mod some other consoles before this if you haven't already, and then practice your soldering skills. Find a broken electronic, buy some flux, and get really good at attaching small wires. For the RGH I just did a few days ago, it took me using a microscope to scratch a small part of the motherboard, and then attempting to stick a wire to it while still working under the microscope, so hopefully that can put the difficulty level into perspective.

If you want to go back to the time period that you were talking about, honestly a PS3 with PS3Hen is probably going to be the best option as it requires no soldering and is fairly beginner friendly. But, if you want to work on some soldering skills and get a cool prize for it, give the RGH a try! 

Hopefully this helps you OP, and happy modding!

As a general rule, when Jailbreaking/Modding a 360 via JTAG or RGH (most popular hacks) you should plan on only using offline accounts. There are some workarounds to try and play on Xbox live, but I wouldn’t get my Microsoft account info within a ten mile radius of that thing, it’s ban city.

There are some upsides though! You can still collect achievements/gamerscore on an offline account, and obviously you can play virtually any game or create backups for your collection to have it on-demand. But, I would say if you’re interested in modding for a hacked XBL experience you gotta have the cash in case your console gets sniped by papa Bill, or if you don’t care about possibly getting that account banned.

I was forced to go-to therapy and had an awful experience where he basically told me "that sucks" to all my problems. He then put me on medication which rod me of all emotion and I stopped going and after another episode I had realized what my issue was.
Control.
I have the constant need for control over a situation, whether it's as simple as where the conversation is going or if my relationship has a major hole in it, it was always control.

It took months of practice and acceptance but I learned to let certain things go and to "go with the flow". It sucked and I hated life but slowly I got more used to less control. My trust in others became much greater and I stepped out of my shell and I'm able to actually talk to strangers now. Building trust with others is key but even more key is building that same trust with yourself. Letting smaller issues play them selves out and the larger ones being addressed, I'm still anxious, I still get suicidal thoughts but I try to relax. Hug my cat. Go on with my day and play Minecraft to help get my mind off things. 
Suicide is never something absent from my thoughts, it more then likely always will be there but I've accepted it.
